column1: # NCLEX additions. Answer, clue, rationale, topic. Tab-separated.

column2: Antiemetic that blocks serotonin receptors and can prolong the QT interval
column3: Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 blocker used for chemo and postoperative nausea. Watch the QT interval.

column2: Benzodiazepine used for anxiety and status epilepticus that depresses breathing
column3: Lorazepam boosts GABA. Watch sedation and respiratory depression, especially with opioids.

column2: Longer-acting benzodiazepine used for seizures, spasms, and alcohol withdrawal
column3: Diazepam is a GABA agonist. It treats seizures, muscle spasm, and alcohol withdrawal.

column2: Short-acting benzodiazepine for anxiety whose abrupt stop can cause withdrawal
column3: Alprazolam is habit-forming. Taper it; sudden stops can cause rebound anxiety or seizures.

column2: First-generation antipsychotic that can cause dystonia and a prolonged QT
column3: Haloperidol treats psychosis and acute agitation. Watch extrapyramidal effects and QT.

column2: SSRI antidepressant that raises serotonin and can cause sexual side effects
column3: Sertraline takes weeks for mood effect. Watch for serotonin syndrome if combined with other serotonergic drugs.

column2: Long half-life SSRI often chosen when a weekly washout reduces withdrawal risk
column3: Fluoxetine has a long half-life. It is an SSRI used for depression and some anxiety disorders.

column2: Antidepressant that lowers the seizure threshold and is avoided in eating disorders
column3: Bupropion does not cause the sexual side effects of SSRIs. Avoid it when seizure risk is high.

column2: Antidepressant often used for sleep that can cause priapism
column3: Trazodone is sedating. Teach patients to report a prolonged painful erection.

column2: Anticonvulsant used for neuropathic pain that is cleared by the kidneys
column3: Gabapentin is renally cleared. Doses are reduced when GFR falls, and sedation is common.

column2: Antiseizure drug that is teratogenic and can injure the liver and pancreas
column3: Valproate is avoided in pregnancy. Monitor liver enzymes, platelets, and signs of pancreatitis.

column2: Antiseizure drug whose serious rash risk rises if the dose is raised too fast
column3: Lamotrigine is titrated slowly. A rash can signal Stevens-Johnson syndrome and the drug is stopped.

column2: Proton pump inhibitor used for ulcer and reflux that can lower magnesium long term
column3: Omeprazole reduces gastric acid. Long courses are linked with low magnesium and C. difficile risk.

column2: H2 blocker that reduces stomach acid and is adjusted when the kidneys are weak
column3: Famotidine blocks histamine at the parietal cell. Reduce the dose in renal impairment.

column2: Mucosal coating agent for ulcers that is given on an empty stomach
column3: Sucralfate forms a barrier over ulcers. Separate it from other oral drugs so it does not bind them.

column2: Stool softener used to prevent straining after surgery or with painful defecation
column3: Docusate pulls water into stool. It prevents constipation; it does not treat a hard impaction alone.

column2: Stimulant laxative used for short-term constipation, often at bedtime
column3: Bisacodyl stimulates the colon. Do not use stimulant laxatives as a daily habit.

column2: Plant stimulant laxative that increases colonic motility
column3: Senna is a stimulant laxative. Abdominal cramping can occur, and long daily use is discouraged.

column2: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor that lowers uric acid and is a maintenance gout drug
column3: Allopurinol prevents gout flares over time. It is not the treatment for an acute joint flare.

column2: Anti-inflammatory used early in acute gout that causes diarrhea at high doses
column3: Colchicine is most useful when started soon after a gout flare. Diarrhea is the dose-limiting effect.

column2: Aminopenicillin used for otitis, sinusitis, and some streptococcal infections
column3: Amoxicillin is a beta-lactam. A rash in mono is common, and true allergy is a contraindication.

column2: First-generation cephalosporin often given before surgery to prevent skin flora infection
column3: Cefazolin is a common perioperative prophylactic antibiotic. It covers many gram-positive skin organisms.

column2: Third-generation cephalosporin used for meningitis, gonorrhea, and serious gram-negative infection
column3: Ceftriaxone reaches the meninges. It is a workhorse for community meningitis and gonorrhea regimens.

column2: Tetracycline used for Lyme disease, acne, and atypical pneumonia that discolors teeth
column3: Doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy and young children because it stains developing teeth.

column2: Lincosamide that covers anaerobes and is strongly linked with C. difficile colitis
column3: Clindamycin treats anaerobic and some gram-positive infections. Diarrhea can mean C. difficile.

column2: Oxazolidinone for resistant gram-positive infection that can cause serotonin syndrome
column3: Linezolid covers MRSA and VRE. It is an MAO inhibitor, so combining it with SSRIs is risky.

column2: Carbapenem reserved for serious resistant infection and covering many anaerobes
column3: Meropenem is a broad carbapenem. It can lower the seizure threshold, especially in renal failure.

column2: Azole antifungal used for candida that inhibits CYP enzymes and raises some drug levels
column3: Fluconazole treats mucosal and systemic candida. It interacts with warfarin and some statins.

column2: Antiviral for herpes that is given with good hydration to protect the kidneys
column3: Acyclovir treats HSV and varicella-zoster. IV doses need hydration because crystals can injure the kidney.

column2: Neuraminidase inhibitor started early to shorten influenza illness
column3: Oseltamivir works best within about 48 hours of flu symptom onset. It is not a substitute for vaccination.

column2: Topical or swish antifungal used for oral thrush that is not systemically absorbed
column3: Nystatin suspension is swished and swallowed for oral candida. It acts locally in the gut and mouth.

column2: Low-molecular-weight heparin dosed by weight and used for clot treatment and prevention
column3: Enoxaparin is given subcutaneously. Dose is reduced in renal impairment, and protamine only partly reverses it.

column2: Antiplatelet prodrug used after stent placement that is stopped before many surgeries
column3: Clopidogrel blocks the P2Y12 receptor. Hold it before elective surgery because of bleeding risk.

column2: Direct oral anticoagulant that inhibits factor Xa and does not need INR checks
column3: Apixaban is used for atrial fibrillation and venous clots. Bleeding is the main risk; INR is not the monitor.

column2: Once-daily factor Xa inhibitor that must be taken with food at the treatment dose
column3: Rivaroxaban 15 and 20 mg doses are taken with food so absorption is adequate.

column2: Direct thrombin inhibitor whose capsules must stay in the original bottle
column3: Dabigatran is moisture sensitive. Do not crush the capsules, and bleeding risk rises with poor renal function.

column2: Antithyroid drug for hyperthyroidism that is avoided in the first trimester
column3: Methimazole blocks thyroid hormone synthesis. Agranulocytosis is a rare emergency signaled by fever or sore throat.

column2: Sulfonylurea that stimulates insulin release and can cause hypoglycemia
column3: Glipizide lowers glucose by pushing the pancreas to release insulin. Teach patients to eat when they take it.

column2: Longer sulfonylurea more likely to cause prolonged hypoglycemia in older adults
column3: Glyburide is generally avoided in older adults because hypoglycemia can last.

column2: DPP-4 inhibitor for type 2 diabetes that is weight neutral and rarely causes hypoglycemia alone
column3: Sitagliptin raises incretin effect. By itself it seldom causes low glucose, unlike sulfonylureas.

column2: Direct arterial vasodilator used for hypertension that can cause reflex tachycardia
column3: Hydralazine drops afterload. Reflex tachycardia and a lupus-like syndrome can occur.

column2: Dihydropyridine calcium blocker for hypertension and angina that causes ankle edema
column3: Amlodipine relaxes arterial smooth muscle. Peripheral edema is common and is not a reason to add a diuretic first.

column2: Non-dihydropyridine calcium blocker that slows the AV node and lowers heart rate
column3: Diltiazem is used for rate control. Avoid it in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

column2: Calcium blocker that slows heart rate and is constipating
column3: Verapamil blocks cardiac calcium channels. Constipation and bradycardia are classic effects.

column2: Central alpha agonist for blood pressure whose sudden stop can cause rebound hypertension
column3: Clonidine is tapered. Abrupt withdrawal can spike the blood pressure.

column2: Short-acting ACE inhibitor that can cause cough, high potassium, and angioedema
column3: Captopril blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme. Stop it for angioedema and avoid it in pregnancy.

column2: ACE inhibitor prodrug used for hypertension and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
column3: Enalapril lowers afterload and mortality in HFrEF. Watch potassium, creatinine, and cough.

column2: Angiotensin receptor blocker used when an ACE inhibitor cough is intolerable
column3: Valsartan blocks the AT1 receptor. It does not cause the bradykinin cough of ACE inhibitors.

column2: Nonselective beta blocker with alpha block used in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
column3: Carvedilol is evidence-based in HFrEF. Start low; it can worsen symptoms if begun during decompensated failure.

column2: Nonselective beta blocker used for tremor, migraine prevention, and thyroid storm symptoms
column3: Propranolol blocks beta-1 and beta-2 receptors. It can worsen asthma and hide hypoglycemia signs.

column2: Combined alpha and beta blocker given IV for severe hypertension in pregnancy
column3: Labetalol lowers blood pressure without the pure beta-blocker rise in systemic resistance. It is used for severe prenatal hypertension.

column2: Antiarrhythmic that contains iodine and can injure the lungs, thyroid, and liver
column3: Amiodarone has a huge half-life. Monitor lungs, thyroid, liver, and eyes during long courses.

column2: Inotrope that stimulates beta-1 receptors and is used in cardiogenic shock
column3: Dobutamine raises contractility. It can provoke tachycardia and ischemia.

column2: Antidiuretic hormone analog used in vasodilatory shock and diabetes insipidus
column3: Vasopressin raises blood pressure in shock and replaces ADH in central diabetes insipidus.

column2: PDE inhibitor inotrope and vasodilator used in advanced heart failure
column3: Milrinone increases contractility and dilates vessels. Hypotension is the limiting effect.

column2: Inhaled anticholinergic bronchodilator used with albuterol in COPD exacerbations
column3: Ipratropium blocks muscarinic receptors in the airway. It is a reliever, not an anti-inflammatory controller.

column2: Leukotriene receptor blocker used for asthma control and allergic rhinitis
column3: Montelukast is a daily controller. Mood changes have been reported and should be taught.

column2: Inhaled corticosteroid controller for asthma that can cause oral thrush
column3: Fluticasone reduces airway inflammation. Rinse the mouth after use to lower candida risk.

column2: Inhaled or nebulized steroid used as an asthma controller and in some croup regimens
column3: Budesonide is an inhaled corticosteroid. It prevents symptoms; it does not replace a rescue bronchodilator.

column2: Oral opioid analgesic that depresses respirations and is reversed by naloxone
column3: Oxycodone is a full opioid agonist. Constipation is expected, and sedation with benzodiazepines is dangerous.

column2: Weak opioid that also raises serotonin and lowers the seizure threshold
column3: Tramadol has opioid and serotonergic effects. Seizures and serotonin syndrome are the teaching points.

column2: Potent NSAID limited to short courses because of kidney injury and bleeding
column3: Ketorolac is for short-term pain. Avoid it in renal failure, peptic ulcer, and late pregnancy.

column2: NSAID that reduces pain and fever and can worsen heart failure and kidneys
column3: Ibuprofen blocks COX. It can raise blood pressure, retain fluid, and cause gastric bleeding.

column2: Longer-acting NSAID used for pain and dysmenorrhea with the usual COX risks
column3: Naproxen shares NSAID risks: gastritis, renal injury, and fluid retention.

column2: Muscle relaxant that is the specific treatment for malignant hyperthermia
column3: Dantrolene blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. It treats malignant hyperthermia.

column2: Drug that raises fetal hemoglobin and reduces sickle cell crises
column3: Hydroxyurea lowers the rate of painful sickle crises. It is myelosuppressive, so blood counts are followed.

column2: Growth factor that raises neutrophils after chemotherapy
column3: Filgrastim stimulates neutrophil production. Bone pain is a common effect.

column2: Vitamin B6 given with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy
column3: Pyridoxine prevents isoniazid neuropathy and is also the antidote for isoniazid overdose seizures.

column2: Anticholinergic used for antipsychotic-induced dystonia and parkinsonism
column3: Benztropine treats acute dystonia. It causes dry mouth, retention, and confusion in older adults.

column2: Dopamine precursor for Parkinson disease that is given with carbidopa
column3: Levodopa crosses into the brain and becomes dopamine. Carbidopa blocks peripheral conversion so less is needed.

column2: Peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor paired with levodopa so more drug reaches the brain
column3: Carbidopa does not cross the blood-brain barrier. It reduces nausea from peripheral dopamine.

column2: Subjective shortness of breath that is assessed before assuming anxiety
column3: Dyspnea is what the patient feels. Measure oxygen, work of breathing, and lung sounds rather than dismissing it.

column2: Abnormally fast respiratory rate that can signal hypoxia, pain, or acidosis
column3: Tachypnea is a vital-sign finding. In metabolic acidosis it may be compensatory, as in Kussmaul breathing.

column2: Coughing up blood, which can occur with tuberculosis, cancer, or pulmonary embolism
column3: Hemoptysis needs airway protection and a search for the source. Massive bleeding is an emergency.

column2: Black tarry stool from digested blood, usually an upper gastrointestinal bleed
column3: Melena suggests blood has been in the gut long enough to be digested. Assess hemodynamics first.

column2: Pain when pressure on the abdomen is released, suggesting peritoneal irritation
column3: Rebound tenderness is a peritoneal sign. It supports processes such as perforation or advanced appendicitis.

column2: Involuntary abdominal muscle tightness over an inflamed peritoneum
column3: Guarding is a peritoneal finding. Pair it with vital signs and a surgical evaluation when it is new.

column2: Fluid in the peritoneal cavity, classically from portal hypertension in cirrhosis
column3: Ascites is assessed by shifting dullness and a fluid wave. A tense abdomen can impair breathing.

column2: Flapping tremor of the hands seen in hepatic encephalopathy
column3: Asterixis is elicited by asking the patient to hold the wrists extended. It supports metabolic encephalopathy.

column2: Itching that can follow cholestasis, opioid use, or uremia
column3: Pruritus in liver disease is from retained bile salts. New itching with a rash also needs a skin and allergy review.

column2: Redness of the skin from vasodilation, seen in infection, allergy, or pressure injury
column3: Erythema that does not blanch over a bony prominence is an early pressure injury.

column2: Purple nonblanching skin lesions from bleeding under the skin
column3: Purpura does not blanch. It can reflect low platelets, vasculitis, or meningococcemia.

column2: Bruise from blood in the soft tissue that changes color as it heals
column3: Ecchymosis after minor trauma can signal a clotting problem when it is extensive or unexplained.

column2: Bulbous fingertips associated with chronic lung disease and some heart shunts
column3: Clubbing develops over time with chronic hypoxemia. It is not an acute finding.

column2: Pale skin or conjunctiva that can reflect anemia or poor perfusion
column3: Pallor of the conjunctiva is a bedside clue to anemia. Pair it with heart rate and hemoglobin.

column2: Yellow skin from elevated bilirubin, seen in hemolysis or liver and bile disease
column3: Jaundice appears when bilirubin is high. Scleral icterus is often noticed first.

column2: Yellow discoloration of the sclera from bilirubin
column3: Icteric sclerae are a sensitive bedside sign of hyperbilirubinemia.

column2: Rhythmic eye jerking that can follow vestibular disease or phenytoin toxicity
column3: Nystagmus has many causes. New nystagmus on phenytoin suggests toxicity.

column2: Double vision that can signal cranial nerve or neuromuscular disease
column3: Diplopia that is new needs a neuro exam. In myasthenia it often fluctuates through the day.

column2: Drooping eyelid seen in cranial nerve III palsy and myasthenia gravis
column3: Ptosis with a dilated pupil suggests a compressive third-nerve lesion and is urgent.

column2: Constricted pupils classically seen with opioids and cholinergic excess
column3: Miosis with slow breathing supports opioid toxicity. The antidote is naloxone.

column2: Dilated pupils seen with anticholinergic toxicity and sympathetic stimulation
column3: Mydriasis with dry flushed skin and delirium fits anticholinergic toxicity.

column2: Unsteady gait from cerebellar, sensory, or drug toxicity causes
column3: Ataxia can follow phenytoin toxicity, alcohol, or posterior circulation stroke.

column2: Language impairment, with Broca producing few words and Wernicke producing fluent nonsense
column3: Aphasia is a cortical sign. Broca aphasia is nonfluent; Wernicke aphasia is fluent but empty.

column2: Slurred speech from weak or uncoordinated speech muscles, not a language problem
column3: Dysarthria is a motor speech problem. The patient understands language, unlike in aphasia.

column2: Weakness of one side of the body, the classic motor pattern of a hemispheric stroke
column3: Hemiparesis localizes above the spinal cord, often to the contralateral cortex or internal capsule.

column2: Pins-and-needles sensation from nerve or metabolic irritation
column3: Paresthesia around the mouth and in the hands can be an early sign of low calcium or respiratory alkalosis.

column2: Rhythmic muscle contraction from upper motor neuron irritation, tested at the ankle
column3: Sustained clonus is a pyramidal sign. In preeclampsia it warns that eclampsia may be near.

column2: Balance test that becomes positive when proprioception or dorsal columns fail
column3: A positive Romberg test means the patient sways or falls when the eyes close. It is a sensory, not cerebellar, test.

column2: Low neutrophil count that turns fever into a possible emergency
column3: Febrile neutropenia needs cultures and prompt antibiotics. Flowers and fresh fruit may be restricted.

column2: Cell fragments required for clotting; a low count raises bleeding risk
column3: Platelets are followed before invasive procedures. Spontaneous bleeding risk rises as the count falls very low.

column2: Storage protein that is low in iron deficiency and high as an acute-phase reactant
column3: A low ferritin supports iron deficiency. Inflammation can raise ferritin even when iron stores are poor.

column2: Small red cells, the usual pattern of iron deficiency and thalassemia
column3: Microcytic anemia has a low MCV. Iron deficiency is the common cause; thalassemia is the classic mimic.

column2: Large red cells seen with B12 or folate deficiency and some drugs
column3: Macrocytic anemia has a high MCV. B12 deficiency also causes neurologic findings that folate deficiency does not.

column2: Autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor that prevents vitamin B12 absorption
column3: Pernicious anemia causes B12 deficiency. Neurologic injury can occur even before severe anemia.

column2: Bone marrow failure causing low red cells, white cells, and platelets together
column3: Aplastic anemia is pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow. Infection and bleeding are the dangers.

column2: Inherited factor deficiency that causes deep joint and muscle bleeding
column3: Hemophilia A lacks factor VIII and hemophilia B lacks factor IX. Bleeding is treated with factor replacement.

column2: Transfusion reaction with fever, back pain, and hemoglobinuria from ABO mismatch
column3: Acute hemolytic reactions are from incompatible blood. Stop the transfusion and keep the line open with saline.

column2: Transfusion reaction causing noncardiogenic pulmonary edema during or soon after a unit
column3: TRALI presents with acute hypoxemia and bilateral infiltrates. It is not treated like fluid overload.

column2: Circulatory overload from transfusion, with hypertension and pulmonary edema
column3: TACO is cardiogenic overload. Slow the blood, give oxygen, and diuretics are often used.

column2: Hemoglobin disorder in which dehydrated or hypoxic cells sickle and block flow
column3: Sickle cell crisis is treated with oxygen, fluids, and pain control. Hydroxyurea reduces crisis frequency.

column2: Hypertensive emergency in spinal cord injury above T6, triggered by a full bladder
column3: Autonomic dysreflexia causes headache and high blood pressure. Sit the patient up and empty the bladder.

column2: Surgical opening of a muscle compartment to save tissue from compartment syndrome
column3: Fasciotomy treats compartment syndrome. The clue before surgery is pain out of proportion and pain on stretch.

column2: Pulling force used to align a fracture that requires the weights to hang freely
column3: Traction weights must hang free. Never lift the weights to move the patient up in bed.

column2: Closed muscle space where swelling can cut off perfusion
column3: Compartment syndrome pain is severe and worse with passive stretch. Pulses can still be present.

column2: Drop in blood pressure or rise in pulse when standing, from volume loss or drugs
column3: Orthostatic vital signs compare lying and standing. A large pulse rise or pressure drop suggests hypovolemia.

column2: Heart rate above 100 in adults that can mean pain, fever, bleeding, or arrhythmia
column3: Tachycardia is a compensatory sign. In shock it often appears before the blood pressure falls.

column2: Slow heart rate that is treated when the patient is hypotensive or symptomatic
column3: Symptomatic bradycardia is treated with atropine first in the usual adult algorithm, then pacing if needed.

column2: Abnormal heart rhythm that may reduce cardiac output
column3: New arrhythmia with chest pain or hypotension is urgent. Check electrolytes, especially potassium and magnesium.

column2: Chest pain from myocardial ischemia that is typically relieved by rest or nitroglycerin
column3: Stable angina is predictable with exertion. Pain at rest or lasting longer suggests an acute coronary syndrome.

column2: Tissue oxygen demand that exceeds supply, the mechanism of angina
column3: Ischemia on the ECG may show ST depression or T-wave inversion. Troponin distinguishes injury from ischemia alone.

column2: Swelling from fluid in the interstitial space, pitting when a fingertip leaves a dent
column3: Pitting edema is graded by depth and how long the pit lasts. In heart failure it is often dependent.

column2: Generalized body edema seen in nephrotic syndrome and severe fluid overload
column3: Anasarca is widespread swelling. Daily weights track the fluid better than the scale of a single limb.

column2: Low red cell mass that causes fatigue, pallor, and tachycardia
column3: Anemia reduces oxygen-carrying capacity. Transfusion decisions use symptoms and the hemoglobin, not a number alone.

column2: Excessive thirst, a classic symptom of hyperglycemia and diabetes insipidus
column3: Polydipsia with polyuria and polyphagia is the classic diabetes triad.

column2: Excessive hunger from cells that cannot use glucose in uncontrolled diabetes
column3: Polyphagia occurs when insulin is absent or ineffective and cells are starved despite high blood sugar.

column2: Glucose in the urine once the renal threshold is exceeded
column3: Glycosuria appears in hyperglycemia. It pulls water with it and contributes to polyuria.

column2: Fruity ketone on the breath of a patient in diabetic ketoacidosis
column3: A fruity breath suggests acetone from ketosis. Confirm with glucose, ketones, and an anion gap.

column2: Accumulation of ketone bodies when fat is burned because glucose cannot enter cells
column3: Ketosis in type 1 diabetes can progress to ketoacidosis. Insulin and fluids are the treatment.

column2: Viral illness that is teratogenic in early pregnancy and prevented by vaccination
column3: Rubella in the first trimester can cause congenital cataracts, heart defects, and deafness.

column2: Any exposure that can malform a fetus, including some drugs and infections
column3: Teratogens are most dangerous in organogenesis. Isotretinoin, warfarin, and valproate are classic drug examples.

column2: Vitamin whose deficiency causes neural tube defects and a macrocytic anemia
column3: Folate is supplemented before conception to reduce neural tube defects. Deficiency does not cause B12 neuropathy.

column2: The first fetal movements the pregnant patient feels
column3: Quickening is usually felt in the second trimester, earlier in people who have been pregnant before.

column2: Descent of the fetus into the pelvis late in pregnancy, easing pressure on the diaphragm
column3: Lightening can make breathing easier and increase pelvic pressure and urinary frequency.

column2: When the widest fetal head diameter has passed the pelvic inlet
column3: Engagement is described with station. A floating head is not engaged.

column2: How far the fetal presenting part is above or below the ischial spines
column3: Station zero is at the ischial spines. Positive stations are closer to delivery.

column2: Thinning of the cervix, reported as a percentage
column3: Effacement and dilation are separate. A primigravida often effaces before she dilates much.

column2: Opening of the cervix in centimeters from closed to ten
column3: Full dilation is 10 cm. Pushing is usually delayed until then unless the patient has an urge and is complete.

column2: When the fetal head remains visible at the vaginal opening between contractions
column3: Crowning means birth is imminent. Support the perineum and prepare to deliver.

column2: Umbilical cord slipping ahead of the presenting part, an obstetric emergency
column3: Cord prolapse cuts off fetal blood flow. Relieve pressure with a hand and deliver urgently.

column2: Premature separation of the placenta with painful bleeding and a tense uterus
column3: Placental abruption is painful. Bleeding may be concealed, so the vital signs can worsen before blood is seen.

column2: Organ of fetal gas exchange; its location and separation are emergency concerns
column3: A placenta covering the cervix is previa. Separation before birth is abruption.

column2: Painless third-trimester bleeding from a placenta that covers the cervix
column3: Placenta previa is painless bleeding. Vaginal exams are avoided until ultrasound locates the placenta.

column2: Protein in the urine, a criterion of preeclampsia when paired with hypertension
column3: Proteinuria plus new hypertension after 20 weeks defines preeclampsia. Headache and visual change are severe features.

column2: Immune globulin given to Rh-negative patients to prevent sensitization
column3: Rh immune globulin is given after sensitizing events and routinely in pregnancy when the patient is Rh negative.

column2: Test that detects antibodies coating red cells, used in hemolytic disease
column3: A direct Coombs test is positive when antibodies are bound to red cells, as in hemolytic disease of the newborn.

column2: Brain injury from very high bilirubin in a newborn
column3: Kernicterus is bilirubin toxicity in the basal ganglia. Severe jaundice is treated before it reaches that point.

column2: Pigment from heme breakdown that causes jaundice when it accumulates
column3: Unconjugated bilirubin in newborns is treated with feeding and phototherapy when it is high.

column2: Newborn startle reflex with arm extension then flexion
column3: The Moro reflex is normal in newborns and disappears in the first months. Asymmetry suggests a nerve or clavicle injury.

column2: Newborn reflex of turning the head toward a stroked cheek
column3: Rooting helps the newborn find the breast. Absence in a term baby is abnormal.

column2: Newborn reflex of sucking when the palate is touched
column3: A poor suck can signal prematurity, neurologic injury, or maternal drug exposure.

column2: Newborn reflex of closing the hand around a finger placed in the palm
column3: The palmar grasp is normal early and later becomes a voluntary reach.

column2: Soft spot on the infant skull; sunken suggests dehydration and bulging suggests pressure
column3: A sunken fontanel fits dehydration. A bulging fontanel with fever suggests meningitis.

column2: Fontanel that bows outward, a sign of raised intracranial pressure in infants
column3: A bulging fontanel is an emergency when it comes with fever, lethargy, or a high-pitched cry.

column2: Soft scalp swelling from birth pressure that crosses suture lines
column3: Caput succedaneum crosses sutures and resolves. A cephalohematoma does not cross sutures.

column2: Temporary overlapping of fetal skull bones from the birth canal
column3: Molding is expected after a vaginal birth and resolves. It is not a fracture.

column2: Fine fetal hair still seen on premature newborns
column3: Lanugo is more abundant in preterm infants. It sheds as the skin matures.

column2: White cheesy coating that protects fetal skin
column3: Vernix is left on the skin after birth when possible. Preterm infants may have more of it.

column2: Tiny white keratin cysts on a newborn face that resolve without treatment
column3: Milia are normal. They are not acne and should not be squeezed.

column2: Breast infection in a lactating patient, treated with emptying and often antibiotics
column3: Mastitis causes a red, painful wedge of breast and fever. Continued breastfeeding or pumping is encouraged.

column2: Postpartum bleeding that soaks a pad quickly or drops the blood pressure
column3: Postpartum hemorrhage is often from uterine atony. Massage the fundus and give a uterotonic.

column2: Soft uterus after birth that signals atony and bleeding risk
column3: A boggy fundus is massaged until firm. Have the patient empty the bladder if the uterus is displaced.

column2: Fundal pressure used to firm an atonic postpartum uterus
column3: Fundal massage expresses clots and stimulates contraction. Support the lower uterus so it is not inverted.

column2: Prostaglandin uterotonic avoided in asthma because it can cause bronchospasm
column3: Carboprost treats uterine atony. Asthma is a contraindication because it can tighten bronchial smooth muscle.

column2: Prostaglandin used for postpartum hemorrhage and cervical ripening
column3: Misoprostol causes uterine contraction. Fever and diarrhea are common effects.

column2: Respiratory virus prevented by yearly vaccine and treated early with a neuraminidase inhibitor
column3: Influenza is droplet spread. Antivirals are most useful early, and vaccination is the prevention.

column2: Whooping cough prevented by vaccination and spread by droplets
column3: Pertussis causes a paroxysmal cough. Close contacts may need prophylaxis, and droplet precautions are used.

column2: Toxin-mediated muscle spasm prevented by immunization and a booster after some wounds
column3: Tetanus spores enter dirty wounds. Immunization status decides whether toxoid or immunoglobulin is added.

column2: Chickenpox virus that requires airborne precautions and is dangerous in pregnancy
column3: Varicella is airborne. Pregnant or immunocompromised exposures may need immunoglobulin.

column2: Airborne viral illness with cough, conjunctivitis, and a descending rash
column3: Measles is extremely contagious and airborne. Vitamin A is used in children, and isolation is required.

column2: Droplet viral illness causing parotid swelling
column3: Mumps is prevented by MMR. Orchitis is a classic complication in adolescents and adults.

column2: Liver inflammation; B and C are blood-borne and A is fecal-oral
column3: Hepatitis B is prevented by vaccine and immune globulin after some exposures. A is spread by contaminated food.

column2: Spore-forming colitis after antibiotics that requires soap and water, not alcohol gel
column3: C. difficile causes watery diarrhea. Contact precautions and soap-and-water handwashing are required.

column2: Highly contagious vomiting illness spread by contact and requiring soap and water
column3: Norovirus spreads fast in shared living settings. Alcohol gel does not reliably kill it.

column2: Mite infestation treated with a skin scabicide and contact precautions
column3: Scabies causes intense itching and burrows. Close contacts are often treated at the same time.

column2: Lice infestation treated with a pediculicide and by cleaning combs and bedding
column3: Pediculosis capitis is head lice. School exclusion rules vary; treatment of the hair is the priority.

column2: Honey-crusted bacterial skin infection common in children
column3: Impetigo is usually staph or strep. It is contagious until treated, and contact precautions apply in care settings.

column2: Spreading skin infection with warmth, redness, and fever
column3: Cellulitis is marked so spread can be judged. Elevate the limb and give antibiotics that cover skin flora.

column2: Bladder infection with dysuria and frequency but usually no fever
column3: Cystitis is a lower UTI. Fever and flank pain suggest the infection has reached the kidney.

column2: Painful urination, a hallmark of urinary tract infection
column3: Dysuria with frequency and urgency suggests cystitis. Rule out vaginitis and sexually transmitted infection when the story differs.

column2: Sudden compelling need to void, common in bladder infection and overactive bladder
column3: Urgency with dysuria points to cystitis. New incontinence in an older adult can be the only infection sign.

column2: Side pain over the kidney, classic for pyelonephritis and stones
column3: Flank pain with fever and urinary symptoms suggests pyelonephritis. Colicky pain radiating to the groin suggests a stone.

column2: Lab that rises when tissues are under-perfused, used in sepsis resuscitation
column3: A high lactate supports hypoperfusion. Repeating it shows whether resuscitation is working.

column2: Specimens drawn before antibiotics when the patient is stable enough to wait a few minutes
column3: Blood cultures before the first antibiotic improve the chance of identifying the organism. Do not delay antibiotics for unstable patients.

column2: Drug such as acetaminophen that lowers fever but does not treat the infection
column3: Antipyretics improve comfort. They do not replace antibiotics when a bacterial source is likely.

column2: Threat of harmful contact, a legal injury even before touching occurs
column3: Assault is the threat. Battery is the unwanted touching. Both are intentional torts.

column2: Unwanted touching, including a procedure performed without consent
column3: Battery includes treating a patient who has refused. Consent is the protection.

column2: Failure to meet the standard of care that causes harm
column3: Negligence needs a duty, a breach, causation, and damages. A near miss without injury is not a completed tort.

column2: Professional negligence by a clinician that injures a patient
column3: Malpractice is negligence applied to professional duty. Documentation of assessments and responses is part of the defense and the care.

column2: False statement that harms reputation; spoken is slander and written is libel
column3: Defamation is a false damaging statement shared with others. Chart objective findings, not labels.

column2: Spoken defamation
column3: Slander is oral. Discussing a patient in a hallway can also breach privacy even when the words are true.

column2: Written defamation
column3: Libel is written. Social media comments about a patient can be both libel and a privacy violation.

column2: Legal duty of nurses to report suspected abuse of children, and often of elders
column3: Mandated reporters must report suspected abuse. Certainty is not required; a reasonable suspicion is enough.

column2: Overriding a patient's choice because the clinician believes it is for their own good
column3: Paternalism conflicts with autonomy. It is rarely justified in a capacitated adult.

column2: Duty to avoid harm, balanced against treatments that have necessary risks
column3: Nonmaleficence means do no harm. Benefits and burdens are weighed with the patient, not imposed.

column2: Fire response order: rescue, alarm, confine, and extinguish
column3: RACE is the fire sequence. Rescue anyone in immediate danger before pulling the alarm and containing the fire.

column2: Walking that prevents clots, atelectasis, and deconditioning after surgery
column3: Early ambulation is a core postoperative intervention. It lowers clot and pneumonia risk.

column2: Elastic stockings that promote venous return and are checked for fit and skin integrity
column3: Antiembolism stockings must be smooth, not rolled, and removed for skin checks.

column2: Spirometer device that encourages deep breaths after surgery
column3: Incentive spirometry prevents atelectasis. Teach a slow inhale and hold, with hourly goals while awake.

column2: Holding a pillow over an incision during coughing to reduce pain
column3: Splinting an abdominal incision makes coughing tolerable so the patient will clear secretions.

column2: Repositioning at intervals to protect skin and mobilize secretions
column3: Turning at least every two hours is the usual pressure-injury schedule, adjusted to the risk score.

column2: Indwelling urinary catheter that is a major source of hospital infection
column3: Foley catheters are removed as soon as they are not needed. Keep the bag below the bladder and the tubing unkinked.

column2: Urinary infection caused by an indwelling catheter
column3: CAUTI prevention is fewer catheters, aseptic insertion, a closed system, and daily review of need.

column2: Bloodstream infection from a central line
column3: CLABSI prevention uses a checklist, sterile insertion, and daily review of whether the line is still needed.

column2: Pneumonia that develops in a patient on a ventilator
column3: Ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention includes elevating the head of the bed and oral care.

column2: Early sepsis actions of lactate, cultures, antibiotics, and fluids
column3: The sepsis bundle is time sensitive. Antibiotics and fluids for hypoperfusion should not wait for a full workup.

column2: Bedside screen using low pressure, fast breathing, and altered mentation
column3: qSOFA flags patients who may have sepsis. It does not replace a full assessment or lactate.

column2: Difference between measured cations and anions, high in ketoacidosis and lactic acidosis
column3: A high anion gap metabolic acidosis is seen in DKA, lactic acidosis, and some ingestions.

column2: Concentration of solute in serum; low in SIADH and high in dehydration
column3: Serum osmolality helps sort hyponatremia. In SIADH it is low while the urine is concentrated.

column2: Low serum sodium that can cause headache, confusion, and seizures
column3: Hyponatremia is corrected carefully. Raising sodium too fast can injure the brain.

column2: High serum sodium from water loss, causing thirst and confusion
column3: Hypernatremia is a water deficit. Replace free water gradually and find the loss.

column2: High potassium that can peak T waves and stop the heart
column3: Severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes is treated with calcium to protect the heart, then insulin with glucose to shift potassium.

column2: Low potassium that causes weakness and U waves and raises digoxin toxicity
column3: Hypokalemia is replaced slowly. IV potassium is never pushed.

column2: Low calcium with tetany, Chvostek sign, and a prolonged QT
column3: Hypocalcemia follows neck surgery and pancreatitis. Calcium is replaced and the airway is watched if tetany is severe.

column2: High calcium that causes stones, bone pain, and psychiatric change
column3: Hypercalcemia is treated with fluids. Malignancy and hyperparathyroidism are classic causes.

column2: Low magnesium that makes potassium hard to correct and can cause torsades
column3: Hypomagnesemia often accompanies low potassium. Replace magnesium or the potassium will not stay up.

column2: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia from a long QT, treated with magnesium
column3: Torsades de pointes is treated with IV magnesium. Stop QT-prolonging drugs.

column2: Separation of a wound edge, often after a strain such as coughing
column3: Dehiscence is managed by keeping the patient still, covering the wound, and calling surgery.

column2: Abdominal organs protruding through a separated incision
column3: Evisceration is an emergency. Cover the bowel with sterile saline gauze and keep the patient supine with knees bent.

column2: Pink wound drainage that is a mix of serum and a little blood
column3: Serosanguineous drainage is often normal early. A sudden gush can mean dehiscence.

column2: Thick opaque drainage that suggests infection
column3: Purulent drainage is cultured when infection is suspected. It is not the same as normal serous fluid.

column2: Bloody drainage that is concerning when it increases
column3: Bright red drainage that soaks a dressing needs a pressure check and a look for bleeding.

column2: Red bumpy healing tissue that means a wound is filling in
column3: Granulation tissue is beefy red. It is protected, not scrubbed away.

column2: Black dead tissue in a wound that often needs removal before healing
column3: Eschar is necrotic. Stable dry eschar on a heel may be left intact; infected eschar is removed.

column2: Yellow stringy dead tissue in a wound bed
column3: Slough is nonviable tissue. It is debrided when the goal is a clean granulating bed.

column2: Pressure injury with intact skin and nonblanchable redness
column3: Stage 1 pressure injury is nonblanchable erythema. Offload the area before the skin opens.

column2: Pressure injury that is a shallow open blister or partial-thickness loss
column3: Stage 2 pressure injury is partial thickness. It is not skin tears or incontinence dermatitis.

column2: Removal of dead tissue so a wound can heal
column3: Debridement may be sharp, enzymatic, or autolytic. Pain control and consent matter before sharp removal.

column2: Removing pressure from a bony prominence or diabetic foot ulcer
column3: Offloading is the treatment of pressure injury. A device that is not worn does not help.

column2: Scale that scores pressure-injury risk from sensation, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction
column3: A low Braden score means high risk. Turning, moisture control, and nutrition are the response.

column2: Fall-risk scale using history, secondary diagnosis, ambulatory aid, IV, gait, and mental status
column3: The Morse score guides fall precautions. A high score means a plan, not a restraint.

column2: Device that alerts staff when a high-risk patient tries to get up
column3: A bed alarm does not prevent the fall by itself. Answer it immediately.

column2: Staff member who stays with a patient who is at immediate risk of harm
column3: A sitter is used for elopement, pulling at lines, or suicide risk when less restrictive options fail.

column2: Bandage or stocking applied without wrinkles to support venous return
column3: Elastic wraps are applied distal to proximal. Check pulses and color after application.

column2: Pneumatic compression devices that squeeze the legs to prevent clots
column3: Sequential compression devices are for patients who are not walking enough. They are not placed on a leg with known acute clot symptoms.

column2: Saline or heparin flush used to keep a peripheral IV patent between doses
column3: A locked IV is flushed on a schedule. Resistance or pain means the site is checked before anything is pushed.

column2: IV fluid leaking into tissue, causing cool swelling at the site
column3: Infiltration is cool edema. Stop the infusion, elevate the limb, and restart elsewhere.

column2: Leak of a vesicant drug into tissue that can cause necrosis
column3: Extravasation of a vesicant is stopped immediately. The antidote and surgical consult depend on the drug.

column2: Red, warm, cordlike vein from an IV that means the catheter comes out
column3: Phlebitis is warm and red along the vein. Remove the catheter and apply warmth.

column2: Operating-room emergency treated by stopping gas, removing the tube, and extinguishing
column3: An airway fire means stop the oxygen, remove the burning tube, and pour saline.

column2: Pause before a procedure to confirm patient, site, and procedure
column3: The time-out is done with the team present. It is not skipped because the room is behind.

column2: Surgeon's mark on the operative site done before sedation when possible
column3: Site marking is done while the patient can participate. The mark is visible after draping.

column2: Colored alert so the team does not give a drug the patient cannot receive
column3: An allergy band is checked against the medication record. Ask what the reaction was, not only the drug name.

column2: Allergy that requires latex-free gloves, catheters, and a careful supply check
column3: Latex allergy can be anaphylaxis. Bananas and kiwis are associated foods, and the room is set up latex free.

column2: Iodinated dye that can injure kidneys and is held around metformin
column3: Contrast nephropathy risk rises with chronic kidney disease. Hydration is the prevention, and metformin is held.

column2: Historical concern that is not a reliable predictor of contrast allergy
column3: A shellfish allergy is not the same as an iodinated-contrast allergy. Ask about prior contrast reactions instead.

column2: Contrast reaction that resembles allergy but is not IgE mediated
column3: Contrast reactions can still cause shock. Treat airway and give epinephrine when the picture is anaphylaxis.

column2: Autoinjector of epinephrine held against the mid-outer thigh for anaphylaxis
column3: Epinephrine for anaphylaxis is intramuscular in the thigh. Teach the patient to carry the device and to call for help after using it.

column2: Emergency kit for severe hypoglycemia when the patient cannot swallow
column3: Glucagon is given when a diabetic patient is unconscious from low glucose and IV dextrose is not available.

column2: Concentrated glucose given IV for severe hypoglycemia in a patient with IV access
column3: IV dextrose raises glucose immediately. Recheck the fingerstick and give a longer-acting carbohydrate once the patient can eat.

column2: Vitamin given before glucose in a malnourished patient to prevent Wernicke injury
column3: Thiamine is given before glucose in suspected Wernicke encephalopathy so glucose does not consume the remaining vitamin.

column2: Triad of confusion, ataxia, and eye-movement palsy from thiamine deficiency
column3: Wernicke encephalopathy is a medical emergency. Give thiamine, especially in alcohol use disorder.

column2: Confabulating amnesia that can follow untreated Wernicke encephalopathy
column3: Korsakoff syndrome is lasting memory loss. Prevention is treating Wernicke early with thiamine.

column2: Acute fluctuating confusion that is a medical symptom, not a dementia diagnosis
column3: Delirium is acute and fluctuating. Find infection, drugs, hypoxia, and urinary retention rather than only sedating the patient.

column2: Chronic progressive cognitive loss that does not fluctuate hour to hour like delirium
column3: Dementia is chronic. A sudden change in a person with dementia is delirium until proven otherwise.

column2: Evening worsening of confusion in dementia
column3: Sundowning is managed with light, routine, and a calm environment. New evening agitation still needs a medical check.

column2: Antipsychotic use in older adults with dementia that raises mortality
column3: Antipsychotics in dementia have a boxed warning. They are not first-line for sundowning.

column2: Devices used only after less restrictive measures fail and an order is obtained
column3: Restraints are a last resort. Assess skin, circulation, and the reason for the device on a schedule, and remove them as soon as it is safe.

column2: Bed rail that can be a restraint when all rails are up to keep a patient from getting out
column3: A full set of side rails used to prevent exit is a restraint. Two rails for turning are usually a mobility aid.

column2: Cushion beside the bed that reduces injury if a patient rolls out
column3: A fall mat reduces injury. It does not replace a plan to answer alarms and to toilet on a schedule.

column2: Scheduled bathroom trips that prevent falls from urgent unassisted walks
column3: Scheduled toileting is a fall intervention. Many falls happen on the way to the bathroom.

column2: Footwear that lowers fall risk compared with socks alone
column3: Nonskid socks or shoes are part of fall precautions. Loose slippers are not.

column2: Belt used to guide a patient during transfers
column3: A gait belt gives a place to hold. Do not lift by the arms or the gown.

column2: Moving a patient with a spinal injury as one unit to protect alignment
column3: Log rolling keeps the spine neutral. It takes more than one person.

column2: Cervical collar kept on until the spine is cleared
column3: A cervical collar is not removed for comfort before the spine is cleared. The jaw-thrust is used if the airway must be opened.

column2: Airway maneuver that avoids extending a possibly injured neck
column3: The jaw thrust opens the airway without a head tilt. It is the choice when spinal injury is possible.

column2: Usual airway opening maneuver when spinal injury is not suspected
column3: The head-tilt chin-lift opens the airway in ordinary collapse. Do not use it when the neck may be injured.

column2: Airway adjunct used only in an unconscious patient without a gag reflex
column3: An oropharyngeal airway triggers vomiting if the gag is intact. Measure from the mouth corner to the earlobe angle.

column2: Soft airway tube tolerated by a patient with a gag, avoided in basilar skull fracture
column3: A nasopharyngeal airway is sized from the nostril to the earlobe. Do not place it when a basilar skull fracture is suspected.

column2: Catheter used to clear secretions, applied on the way out and for a short pass
column3: Suctioning is intermittent and brief. Oxygenate before and after, and stop if the heart rate drops.

column2: Rigid suction tip used for the mouth
column3: A Yankauer clears the oropharynx. It is not advanced deep into the trachea.

column2: Skull fracture suggested by Battle sign or raccoon eyes and CSF from the ear or nose
column3: Basilar skull fracture clues include mastoid bruising and periorbital bruising. Nothing is inserted into the nose.

column2: Periorbital bruising that suggests a basilar skull fracture
column3: Raccoon eyes develop after injury. They are not an immediate bruise from a simple nasal hit.

column2: Mastoid bruising that suggests a basilar skull fracture
column3: Battle sign is postauricular ecchymosis. It may appear hours after the injury.

column2: Ring of blood with a yellow center on linen, suggesting cerebrospinal fluid
column3: A halo on the sheet can mean CSF mixed with blood. Do not pack the nose or ear.

column2: Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular breathing from high intracranial pressure
column3: Cushing triad is a late sign of herniation. Raise the head of the bed and call for help before it appears if pressure is rising.

column2: Osmotic diuretic that pulls fluid from the brain and is filtered for crystals
column3: Mannitol lowers intracranial pressure. Use a filter and watch serum osmolality and sodium.

column2: Brief reduction of carbon dioxide that constricts cerebral vessels in herniation
column3: Short-term hyperventilation is a bridge in herniation. Prolonged low carbon dioxide worsens cerebral ischemia.

column2: Side-lying position and padded rails during a seizure, without objects in the mouth
column3: During a seizure, protect the head, turn the patient, and do not insert a bite block. Time the event.

column2: Continuous seizure activity that is a medical emergency treated with benzodiazepines then a longer antiseizure drug
column3: Status epilepticus is treated immediately with a benzodiazepine, then a drug such as levetiracetam, valproate, or phenytoin.

column2: Confused sleepy period after a seizure
column3: The postictal state is expected. A new focal deficit that does not resolve needs stroke evaluation.

column2: Warning sensation some patients feel before a seizure
column3: An aura can be a smell, a feeling, or a visual change. Teach patients to get to a safe position.

column2: Brief staring seizure, often in children, without a convulsion
column3: Absence seizures look like daydreaming. They are not treated like a tantrum.

column2: Antiseizure drug with few liver interactions that can cause irritability
column3: Levetiracetam is widely used because it has few drug interactions. Mood changes are the side effect to teach.

column2: Antiseizure level that is interpreted with albumin because the drug is highly protein bound
column3: Phenytoin toxicity causes nystagmus and ataxia. A low albumin raises the free level even if the total looks normal.

column2: Gum overgrowth that is a classic long-term effect of phenytoin
column3: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia. Oral care does not fully prevent it but limits inflammation.

column2: Target lab for warfarin that is usually about 2 to 3 for most indications
column3: Warfarin is adjusted to the INR. Vitamin K is the reversal approach for serious bleeding, along with clotting factors when needed.

column2: Fat-soluble vitamin that reverses warfarin and must be consistent in the diet
column3: Vitamin K in food does not have to be avoided; it has to be steady. Sudden binges of greens drop the INR.

column2: Pharmaceutical vitamin K given for excessive warfarin effect
column3: Phytonadione is vitamin K. IV doses are given slowly because rapid injection can cause a severe reaction.

column2: Basic protein that reverses heparin
column3: Protamine reverses unfractionated heparin. Give it slowly; rapid infusion can cause hypotension.

column2: Plasma product that replaces clotting factors
column3: Fresh frozen plasma replaces factors. It is used for bleeding with a coagulopathy, not as a routine volume expander.

column2: Blood product rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, and von Willebrand factor
column3: Cryoprecipitate is given for low fibrinogen, as in DIC with bleeding.

column2: Transfusion used for bleeding or a very low platelet count
column3: Platelets are given for bleeding with thrombocytopenia. They are not useful in TTP, where transfusion can worsen clotting.

column2: Test that determines blood type and looks for antibodies before a possible transfusion
column3: A type and screen is drawn before surgery when transfusion is possible. It is not the same as crossmatching units.

column2: Final compatibility test between donor red cells and the recipient
column3: A crossmatch is done before packed red cells are issued when time allows. Emergency blood may be uncrossmatched O negative.

column2: Universal donor red cells used in life-threatening bleeding before the type is known
column3: O negative red cells are the emergency donor type. Rh-negative patients, especially those who could become pregnant, should not be switched to positive blood casually.

column2: Plasma type that can be given to any recipient in an emergency
column3: AB plasma is the universal plasma donor because it has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies.

column2: Common transfusion reaction with a temperature rise and no hemolysis
column3: A febrile reaction still means the transfusion stops until hemolysis is excluded. Acetaminophen may be used once it is safe to continue a different unit.

column2: Hives during transfusion that may allow restart after an antihistamine if that is the only finding
column3: Mild urticaria can be an allergic transfusion reaction. Stop, assess, and follow protocol before any restart.

column2: No urine output, a late and serious sign of renal failure or obstruction
column3: Anuria means almost no urine. Check the catheter for a kink before assuming the kidneys have stopped.

column2: High urine output that can mean diuresis, hyperglycemia, or diabetes insipidus
column3: Polyuria is interpreted with the serum sodium. In diabetes insipidus the urine is dilute and the sodium rises.

column2: Urine concentration measure that is high when the kidneys conserve water
column3: High specific gravity means concentrated urine, as in dehydration. It is inappropriately high in SIADH.

column2: Cylindrical urine sediment; red cell casts suggest glomerulonephritis
column3: Red cell casts point to glomerular bleeding. Muddy brown casts suggest acute tubular necrosis.

column2: High BUN and creatinine from reduced filtration
column3: Azotemia is the lab picture of reduced GFR. It is prerenal, intrinsic, or postrenal until sorted out.

column2: Kidney injury from poor perfusion, with a high BUN-to-creatinine ratio
column3: Prerenal azotemia improves when perfusion is restored. The kidneys are conserving sodium and water.

column2: Kidney injury from obstruction, such as a stone or a blocked catheter
column3: Postrenal failure is relieved by removing the blockage. Ultrasound looks for hydronephrosis.

column2: Dilation of the renal collecting system from obstruction
column3: Hydronephrosis on ultrasound supports obstruction. Relieve it before the kidney is permanently injured.

column2: Rising creatinine that means filtration has fallen
column3: A rising creatinine is a late marker. Urine output often falls first.

column2: Urine output under about 0.5 milliliters per kilogram per hour in an adult
column3: Oliguria is an early perfusion sign. Check volume status, blood pressure, and catheter patency.

column2: Weight gain, crackles, and edema from too much intake or too little output
column3: Fluid overload is treated by stopping extra fluid, giving diuretics when the kidneys respond, and supporting breathing.

column2: Best bedside measure of fluid balance, taken at the same time each day
column3: Daily weights use the same scale and clothing. A rapid gain is fluid until proven otherwise.

column2: Running total of fluid in and fluid out, including drains and urine
column3: Intake and output catches trends before the weight does if it is recorded completely. Ice chips and IV flushes count.

column2: Fluid shifted out of the vessels into tissues or cavities, as in burns and pancreatitis
column3: Third spacing causes intravascular depletion despite edema. The patient can be hypovolemic and swollen.

column2: Low plasma protein that lets fluid leak into tissues
column3: Low albumin contributes to edema. It is seen in liver failure, nephrotic syndrome, and malnutrition.

column2: Pressure from plasma proteins that holds fluid inside vessels
column3: Oncotic pressure falls when albumin is low, and edema follows.

column2: Pressure from the blood column that pushes fluid out of capillaries
column3: High hydrostatic pressure in heart failure pushes fluid into the lungs and legs.

column2: Inspiratory sounds at the lung bases from fluid or atelectasis
column3: Basilar crackles in heart failure do not clear with a cough the way atelectatic crackles may.

column2: Musical expiratory sound from narrowed airways
column3: Wheezing is airway narrowing, as in asthma or COPD. A silent chest after wheezing can mean airflow has nearly stopped.

column2: Inspiratory sound of upper airway obstruction
column3: Inspiratory stridor is an airway emergency. Do not leave the patient to fetch equipment.

column2: Coarse sounds from secretions in large airways that may clear with coughing
column3: Rhonchi suggest mucus. Have the patient cough and suction if they cannot clear it.

column2: Scratchy sound from inflamed pleura or pericardium
column3: A pleural friction rub is heard with pleuritis. A pericardial rub can mean pericarditis.

column2: Inflammation of the pericardium with pain that is worse lying flat and better sitting forward
column3: Pericarditis pain is positional. Diffuse ST elevation can be seen, and NSAIDs are typical treatment when it is idiopathic.

column2: Compression of the heart by pericardial fluid, with low pressure and distended neck veins
column3: Tamponade is Beck triad: hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled sounds. Fluids are a bridge to drainage.

column2: Exaggerated drop in systolic pressure during inspiration, seen in tamponade
column3: Pulsus paradoxus supports tamponade and severe asthma. It is an exaggerated inspiratory pressure drop.

column2: Visible jugular veins from high right-sided pressure
column3: Jugular venous distention is assessed with the head of the bed raised. It fits heart failure, tamponade, and tension pneumothorax.

column2: Sustained lift of the chest wall from an enlarged ventricle
column3: A precordial heave suggests ventricular enlargement. It is a palpation finding, not a murmur.

column2: Palpable vibration from turbulent flow, often over a stenotic valve or a dialysis fistula
column3: A thrill is turbulent flow you can feel. A new loss of a fistula thrill is an emergency.

column2: Whooshing sound of turbulent flow heard with the bell or diaphragm
column3: A carotid bruit suggests stenosis. A fistula bruit is expected; its absence is not.

column2: Surgically joined artery and vein for dialysis that must not be used for routine blood pressures
column3: A dialysis fistula is assessed for thrill and bruit. No blood pressures or venipunctures on that arm.

column2: Ischemia of the hand distal to a dialysis access
column3: Dialysis access can steal arterial flow. A cold painful hand is reported immediately.

column2: Neurologic symptoms during hemodialysis from a rapid solute shift
column3: Dialysis disequilibrium causes headache and confusion. The treatment is to slow the shift, not to ignore it.

column2: Target weight after dialysis, used to judge fluid removal
column3: Dry weight is the edema-free weight. Removing far below it causes cramps and hypotension.

column2: Cloudy dialysate and abdominal pain in a patient on peritoneal dialysis
column3: Peritonitis in peritoneal dialysis shows cloudy fluid. The fluid is cultured and antibiotics are added to the exchanges.

column2: Sodium polystyrene resin that removes potassium through the gut, slowly
column3: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate lowers potassium over hours. It is not the emergency treatment for ECG changes.

column2: Insulin with glucose that shifts potassium into cells
column3: Insulin drives potassium intracellularly. Glucose is given with it unless the patient is already hyperglycemic.

column2: Intravenous calcium that stabilizes the heart in severe hyperkalemia
column3: Calcium gluconate protects the myocardium from high potassium. It does not lower the potassium.

column2: High-dose inhaled beta agonist that also shifts potassium into cells
column3: Nebulized albuterol can lower potassium temporarily. It is an adjunct, not the only treatment.

column2: Dietary teaching to avoid salt substitutes and some fruits when potassium is high
column3: Salt substitutes are often potassium chloride. Patients with high potassium are taught which foods and substitutes to limit.

column2: Eating pattern rich in produce and low in sodium that lowers blood pressure
column3: The DASH pattern emphasizes vegetables, fruit, and low-fat dairy and limits sodium. It is a blood pressure intervention.

column2: Limit on daily intake used in hyponatremia from SIADH and in some heart failure
column3: Fluid restriction is a first treatment for mild SIADH. The patient needs to know that ice and soup count.

column2: Limit on salt used in hypertension and heart failure
column3: Sodium restriction reduces fluid retention. Teach label reading, not only the salt shaker.

column2: Matching insulin to the grams of carbohydrate in a meal
column3: Carbohydrate counting lets mealtime insulin match intake. The nurse confirms the patient can do the arithmetic.

column2: Diabetes plan to keep taking insulin, check glucose often, and drink fluids during illness
column3: Sick-day rules prevent ketoacidosis. Illness raises glucose even when the patient is not eating, so insulin is not simply skipped.

column2: Daily inspection of diabetic feet for sores the patient may not feel
column3: Daily foot checks prevent amputation. Patients with neuropathy cannot rely on pain to find a wound.

column2: Nylon fiber used to test protective sensation on the sole
column3: A 10-gram monofilament that is not felt means loss of protective sensation and a high ulcer risk.

column2: Rule that clear rapid or regular insulin is drawn before cloudy NPH
column3: When mixing, draw the clear insulin first so the NPH vial is not contaminated with a long-acting suspension error. NPH is the cloudy one.

column2: Long-acting insulin that is not mixed with other insulins
column3: Insulin glargine has no peak and is not mixed in the same syringe with other insulins.

column2: Rapid insulin given with the meal because it starts working within minutes
column3: Lispro is a mealtime insulin. Giving it and then delaying the tray causes hypoglycemia.

column2: Intermediate insulin with a pronounced peak that requires a food plan
column3: NPH peaks several hours after injection. A bedtime dose can cause overnight hypoglycemia.

column2: Low glucose treated with 15 grams of fast carbohydrate if the patient can swallow
column3: The rule of 15 is juice or glucose tabs, a recheck, and a repeat if still low. Unconscious patients get glucagon or IV dextrose.

column2: Early-morning hyperglycemia from growth hormone and cortisol
column3: The dawn phenomenon is a morning rise in glucose. It is not the same as rebound hyperglycemia after an overnight low.

column2: Morning hyperglycemia that follows an unnoticed overnight low
column3: The Somogyi effect is rebound high glucose after nocturnal hypoglycemia. A 3 a.m. check separates it from the dawn phenomenon.

column2: Lab that reflects average glucose over about three months
column3: Hemoglobin A1C tracks long-term glucose. It is less reliable in anemia and hemoglobin variants.

column2: Biguanide paused around iodinated contrast and in severe kidney disease
column3: Metformin is held when the kidneys cannot clear it, including around contrast, because of lactic acidosis risk.

column2: Acidosis from metformin, shock, or ischemia, with a high lactate and no ketones required
column3: Lactic acidosis has a high anion gap and a high lactate. Treat the cause and support perfusion.

column2: Diabetic emergency treated with fluids first, then insulin, and potassium replacement
column3: DKA treatment starts with isotonic fluid. Insulin is started after potassium is known, because insulin drives potassium down.

column2: Hyperosmolar state in type 2 diabetes with very high glucose and little ketoacidosis
column3: HHS has extreme glucose and dehydration without major ketones. Fluid replacement is the core treatment.

column2: Life-threatening hyperthyroidism with fever, tachycardia, and agitation
column3: Thyroid storm is treated with a beta blocker, a thionamide, iodine after the thionamide, and steroids.

column2: Severe hypothyroidism with hypothermia and falling consciousness
column3: Myxedema coma needs airway support, warming, and IV thyroid hormone. It is precipitated by infection or cold.

column2: Acute adrenal failure with shock, low sodium, and high potassium
column3: Adrenal crisis is treated with IV hydrocortisone and fluids. It can follow abrupt steroid withdrawal.

column2: Slow reduction of corticosteroids so the adrenal glands can recover
column3: Long steroid courses are tapered. Stopping suddenly can cause adrenal crisis.

column2: Moon face, truncal obesity, and high glucose from cortisol excess
column3: Cushing syndrome raises infection risk and glucose. It can be from steroids or from the body making too much cortisol.

column2: Adrenal tumor that releases bursts of catecholamines and causes paroxysmal hypertension
column3: Pheochromocytoma causes headache, palpitations, and sweating. Beta blockade is not started before alpha blockade.

column2: Excess ADH treated first with fluid restriction when symptoms are mild
column3: SIADH has low sodium, low serum osmolality, and concentrated urine. Severe symptoms may need hypertonic saline.

column2: Lack of ADH effect causing huge volumes of dilute urine and a rising sodium
column3: Diabetes insipidus produces dilute urine. Central disease is treated with desmopressin; nephrogenic disease is not.

column2: ADH analog used for central diabetes insipidus and some bleeding disorders
column3: Desmopressin replaces ADH in central diabetes insipidus. Too much causes water retention and low sodium.

column2: Uterotonic that can cause water intoxication and too-frequent contractions
column3: Oxytocin is titrated to contractions. Tachysystole reduces fetal oxygen and the infusion is slowed.

column2: Loss of reflexes, low respirations, and a magnesium level that is too high
column3: Magnesium toxicity is treated by stopping the infusion and giving calcium gluconate. Reflexes are checked on a schedule.

column2: Antidote for magnesium toxicity
column3: Calcium gluconate reverses magnesium toxicity. It is kept at the bedside during magnesium infusions for preeclampsia.

column2: Beta agonist tocolytic that can cause maternal tachycardia
column3: Terbutaline relaxes the uterus. Hold it for a high maternal heart rate or pulmonary edema.

column2: Calcium blocker sometimes used to relax the uterus
column3: Nifedipine is a tocolytic option. Blood pressure is watched because it is a vasodilator.

column2: Steroid given to the mother to speed fetal lung maturity
column3: Betamethasone is given when preterm birth is likely. It reduces neonatal respiratory distress.

column2: Medications used to delay preterm labor long enough to give steroids
column3: Tocolysis buys time. It is not used when the mother or fetus is unstable or the cervix is far advanced in some protocols.

column2: Monitoring strip interpreted for baseline, variability, and decelerations
column3: Fetal heart rate variability is reassuring. Late decelerations suggest uteroplacental insufficiency.

column2: Deceleration that starts after the contraction peak and signals poor placental perfusion
column3: Late decelerations are treated by position change, oxygen, stopping oxytocin, and fluids, then delivery if they persist.

column2: Abrupt deceleration from cord compression
column3: Variable decelerations are often relieved by position change. Deep prolonged ones can mean cord prolapse.

column2: Deceleration that mirrors the contraction and is caused by head compression
column3: Early decelerations are usually benign. They start and end with the contraction.

column2: Rise in fetal heart rate that is reassuring
column3: Accelerations mean the fetus is oxygenated and neurologically responsive. Their absence needs context, not panic by itself.

column2: Antepartum test in which accelerations are the desired finding
column3: A reactive nonstress test has accelerations. A nonreactive test leads to further evaluation, not an automatic diagnosis of distress.

column2: Ultrasound score of fetal movement, tone, breathing, fluid, plus the nonstress test
column3: The biophysical profile scores fetal well-being. Low amniotic fluid is a concerning component.

column2: Fluid around the fetus; too little suggests placental problems or rupture
column3: Oligohydramnios is low fluid. It can follow rupture of membranes or poor placental function.

column2: Fetal stool in the fluid that can be inhaled and cause respiratory distress
column3: Meconium-stained fluid means the resuscitation team is ready. Routine deep suction of a vigorous newborn is not required.

column2: Delivery emergency in which the anterior shoulder is stuck behind the pubic bone
column3: Shoulder dystocia maneuvers include McRoberts flexion of the maternal thighs and suprapubic pressure. Fundal pressure is not used.

column2: Maternal thigh flexion that opens the pelvis during shoulder dystocia
column3: McRoberts position is the first maneuver for shoulder dystocia. It is paired with suprapubic, not fundal, pressure.

column2: Newborn score that guides resuscitation and is repeated if it is low
column3: A low Apgar score prompts support of airway and breathing. It does not by itself predict long-term development.

column2: Keeping a newborn warm because cold stress raises oxygen and glucose use
column3: Newborns lose heat quickly. Dry, hat, and skin-to-skin or a warmer prevent cold stress.

column2: Low glucose in a newborn, especially infants of diabetic mothers and preterm infants
column3: Neonatal hypoglycemia is treated with feeding or IV glucose. Jitteriness and a weak cry are clues.

column2: Injection given to newborns to prevent hemorrhagic disease
column3: Newborns have low vitamin K. An IM dose prevents bleeding.

column2: Eye ointment given to newborns to prevent gonococcal conjunctivitis
column3: Erythromycin eye prophylaxis prevents ophthalmia neonatorum. It does not treat an established infection by itself.

column2: Newborn test done before discharge because hearing loss is invisible
column3: Universal hearing screening finds loss before speech is delayed. A referral is not a final diagnosis.

column2: Newborn screen for phenylketonuria, drawn after feeding has started
column3: The metabolic screen includes phenylketonuria. It is collected after protein feeding so metabolites are present.

column2: Procedure after which bleeding and first void are checked
column3: After circumcision, the site is checked for bleeding and the infant must void. Petroleum gauze is used with the Gomco or Mogen method teaching.

column2: Keeping the umbilical stump clean and dry until it falls off
column3: Cord care is fold the diaper below the stump and report redness or drainage. Alcohol routines vary; dryness is the goal.

column2: Bilirubin rise that appears in the first day and is not a normal pattern
column3: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathologic. It needs a bilirubin level and a cause, not watchful waiting.

column2: Jaundice that appears after the first day and peaks in the typical newborn pattern
column3: Physiologic jaundice is later and milder than pathologic jaundice. It still needs a level if it looks significant.

column2: Blue-green light that converts bilirubin into a form the newborn can excrete
column3: Phototherapy protects the eyes and monitors temperature and hydration. Lights are not stopped for long feeding breaks if the level is high.

column2: Procedure that replaces newborn blood when bilirubin is dangerously high
column3: Exchange transfusion is for severe hyperbilirubinemia not controlled by phototherapy. It is done in a neonatal unit.

column2: Feeding through a tube when a newborn cannot safely suck and swallow
column3: Gavage feeding checks tube placement before each feed. Residual volume is assessed per unit policy.

column2: Opening in the palate that affects feeding and later speech
column3: Cleft palate feeding uses special nipples. Surgery is planned with a team; feeding is the newborn priority.

column2: Congenital connection that causes choking with feeds and requires surgery
column3: Tracheoesophageal fistula presents with coughing during feeds and a prenatal polyhydramnios history. The infant is kept NPO.

column2: Infantile gastric outlet obstruction with projectile nonbilious vomiting
column3: Pyloric stenosis causes projectile vomiting and an olive-like mass. Electrolytes are corrected before surgery.

column2: Telescoping bowel causing intermittent pain and currant-jelly stool
column3: Intussusception causes episodic pain and a sausage mass. An air enema is often both diagnostic and therapeutic.

column2: Missing ganglion cells causing failure to pass meconium and a tight rectal segment
column3: Hirschsprung disease presents with delayed meconium and a distended abdomen. A rectal biopsy confirms it.

column2: Gluten-sensitive enteropathy with foul stools and poor growth
column3: Celiac disease is treated with a strict gluten-free diet. Diagnosis is confirmed before the diet is started when possible.

column2: Genetic disease with thick mucus, salty sweat, and malabsorption
column3: Cystic fibrosis affects lungs and pancreas. Airway clearance and pancreatic enzymes are daily care.

column2: Test that is high in cystic fibrosis
column3: A high sweat chloride supports cystic fibrosis. Genetic testing confirms the mutations.

column2: Replacement capsules taken with meals in cystic fibrosis and chronic pancreatitis
column3: Pancreatic enzymes are taken with food so fat is absorbed. They are not crushed into a formula that will be heated.

column2: Childhood vasculitis with fever, rash, strawberry tongue, and coronary risk
column3: Kawasaki disease is treated with IV immunoglobulin and aspirin. The coronary arteries are the concern.

column2: Red tongue with prominent papillae seen in Kawasaki disease and scarlet fever
column3: A strawberry tongue is a clue, not a diagnosis. Fever pattern and the rest of the exam decide the illness.

column2: Sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue after group A strep
column3: Scarlet fever is treated as streptococcal infection. The rash does not mean the antibiotics can wait.

column2: Immune sequela of strep throat that can scar heart valves
column3: Rheumatic fever follows untreated strep. Prevention is treating streptococcal pharyngitis.

column2: Middle-ear infection with a bulging tympanic membrane
column3: Acute otitis media is common after a cold. Treatment depends on age and severity; pain control is always part of it.

column2: Drooling, tripod position, and a thumbprint epiglottis; do not examine the throat
column3: Epiglottitis is an airway emergency. Keep the child calm and do not use a tongue blade.

column2: Barking cough and steeple sign treated with humidified air, steroid, and racemic epinephrine if severe
column3: Croup is viral subglottic swelling. Stridor at rest is more serious than a bark alone.

column2: Infant wheezing illness, usually from RSV, managed with support and oxygen
column3: Bronchiolitis is suction and oxygen. Routine bronchodilators and steroids are not the main treatment.

column2: Viral bronchiolitis that spreads by contact and requires precautions
column3: RSV is contact spread. High-risk infants may receive preventive antibody during the season.

column2: Written plan that tells a family when to step up inhalers
column3: An asthma action plan uses symptoms and peak flow zones. Families should be able to teach it back.

column2: Home device that shows airway narrowing before symptoms are severe
column3: Peak flow is compared with the patient's personal best. A drop into the red zone means the rescue plan.
